analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers file federal returns for free directly through the IRS website.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Treasury Department to let individual taxpayers file their federal income tax returns electronically straight through the IRS website, with no commercial middleman charging a fee [S2] [S3]. It set a deadline of no later than three years after enactment, ordered a public education campaign so people knew the option existed, and required the IRS to report to Congress twice a year on progress and once a year on how many people used it [S3]. Today, most Americans who e-file do so through commercial software that charges a fee or steers users toward paid upgrades.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers who currently pay commercial software or preparers to file, or who navigate 'free' commercial programs that push paid add-ons, would get a genuinely free, direct filing option from the government.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Treasury Secretary to let individual taxpayers file federal income tax returns electronically through the IRS website without using any intermediary [S2] [S3].
Requires the program to be running for tax years beginning no later than three years after enactment, and orders a public information and consumer education campaign to tell taxpayers about it [S3].
Requires the IRS to report to Congress every six months on implementation and annually, with the National Taxpayer Advocate, on taxpayer usage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through an open-ended appropriation to build and run the IRS's own filing system; commercial tax software and preparation firms would lose the revenue from filers who switch to the free option.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers generally, and tax software firms

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes 'such sums as are necessary' with no cost estimate or cap for building and maintaining the system, leaving its price tag open [S3].

It would put the IRS in the filing business alongside private software companies, a change critics argued duplicates products already offered, including the existing IRS Free File program run through commercial partners [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is a real, permanent saving for anyone who now pays to file or gets upsold inside 'free' commercial products, though the bill leaves the government's development and maintenance cost uncapped and the design details to the Treasury Secretary. A reasonable objection is cost control; the counterweight is that the government already stores and processes every return and, in 2008, already ran a limited Free File program through industry partners. On balance the bill addressed a real annual cost to households, but it died before anyone estimated the bill's specific price or drafted a serious version.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2009 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Lampson and five original cosponsors introduced the bill on April 15, 2008, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
Nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no action was ever taken after the referral [S4] [S5].
The bill received no hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial tax preparation and software companies keep the market for paid electronic filing, and taxpayers keep paying for it or navigating free-file products built around paid upgrades.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tax software firms kept their market

for.name: Nick Lampson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Free Internet Filing Act on April 15, 2008

against.name: Charlie Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Commercial tax preparation software companies
against.what_they_did: Opposed direct government-run free e-filing and lobbied against proposals like it

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters listed on the bill were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where broader party positions could show [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Tax preparation software and services companies
industries.note: These companies charge many households tens of dollars or more per return, and their 'free' products steer filers toward paid state returns and add-ons. A direct, free IRS filing channel would let people bypass them entirely; the bill even allowed the IRS to contract with an intermediary for free universal access, so firms could not charge filers but could compete to run the government channel [S3].

industries.industry: Paid tax preparers (chains and independent preparers)
industries.note: Filers who currently pay a preparer could use the free government option instead, costing preparers business, though many filers with complex returns would still want professional help.
